We must weigh the tangible asset we would gain against the intangible but very real delay in other work.

To: Engineering Leadership
From: Infrastructure Working Group
Subject: Local AI hardware: expand or optimise?

We are at a decision point about our local AI compute. The question sounds simple, but it is really about how we want to balance cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility over the next year. This memo lays out our thinking and ends with a clear recommendation, while being honest about the uncertainty that remains.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward. If we add capacity, we can run more experiments in parallel, shorten queues, and reduce the risk that a single failure stalls multiple teams. More hardware can also improve tail latency, because jobs are less likely to be squeezed behind a long-running task. The downside is that capital is expensive, and it is committed up front. We would be paying for peak utilisation that may never materialise, and we would be locking ourselves into a particular vendor, form factor, and power profile. If our workloads shift, that hardware could become a stranded asset. There is also a hidden reliability risk: more machines means more things to fail, more firmware to patch, and more operational burden on a small team.

The case for improving utilisation is subtler. Today, we have idle cycles, fragmented scheduling, and some jobs that hold resources for longer than they need to. If we can make better use of what we own, we may defer or avoid a purchase entirely. This path is cheaper, and it is reversible. We can try new schedulers, better batching, or smarter placement of inference and training jobs, and we can roll back if the results disappoint. The risk is that we may not move the needle enough. Utilisation work is often incremental, and it can consume engineering time that we might need elsewhere. There is also a latency tradeoff: if we pack workloads too tightly, we can increase contention and make tail latency worse, which may hurt the very experiments we are trying to accelerate.

When we weigh these options, the opportunity cost is central. Every hour our engineers spend tuning the cluster is an hour they are not spending on product work. Every dollar we spend on hardware is a dollar we cannot spend on data, tooling, or hiring. The question is not simply “can we afford more hardware,” but “is hardware the highest-value use of our next dollar and our next engineer-month?” Our current evidence suggests that we do not yet have a clear, sustained saturation problem. We see occasional queue delays, but they are not yet a systemic bottleneck. That points us toward optimisation first.

Our recommendation is to invest in utilisation improvements now, and to defer any hardware purchase until we have measured the effect. Specifically, we should spend the next quarter on better scheduling, more aggressive batching for inference, and clearer policies for resource allocation. We should instrument the cluster so that we can see utilisation, tail latency, and failure rates in near real time. If, after that work, we still see sustained saturation and unacceptable tail latency, we can revisit the hardware question with much better data.

We want to be candid about uncertainty. We do not know how quickly our workloads will grow, and we do not know whether the utilisation gains will be enough. It is possible that a small hardware purchase would pay for itself in engineer time, and it is possible that our optimisation work will stall. To manage that uncertainty, we favour reversible, low-commitment actions. We should avoid long-term contracts or large upfront orders until the data justifies them. If we do decide to buy later, we should prefer configurations that can be incrementally expanded, and we should keep a clear exit path if the economics change.

In short, we recommend improving utilisation before buying more hardware. This path is cheaper, it is more reversible, and it respects the opportunity cost of our limited engineering attention. It also gives us the information we need to make a confident hardware decision later, if and when it becomes necessary. We ask for leadership’s support to proceed on this basis, with a clear checkpoint at the end of the quarter to review the results and decide whether to revisit the hardware question.

To: Engineering Leadership
From: Infrastructure Working Group
Subject: Local AI Hardware Acquisition vs. Utilisation Improvement
Date: [Current Date]

We are at a decision point that will shape our AI capabilities for the next two to three years. The question before us is whether to purchase additional local AI hardware or to invest our engineering effort into improving the utilisation of the systems we already own. This is not merely a procurement decision; it is a statement about how we value our time, our capital, and our strategic flexibility.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward. We have observed queue times for our most demanding workloads, and adding capacity would immediately relieve that pressure. Newer hardware would also bring efficiency gains at the silicon level, potentially lowering our cost per inference. However, this path carries significant hidden costs. The upfront capital expenditure is substantial, and it commits us to a specific vendor’s roadmap and pricing model. We would also inherit the operational burden of provisioning, patching, and eventually decommissioning that hardware. Perhaps most importantly, we would be making this decision under uncertainty. Our workload mix is shifting as we experiment with new model architectures, and we risk over-provisioning for a future that may not materialise, or under-provisioning in ways that only become painfully clear after the purchase is irreversible.

The alternative is to treat our existing fleet as a fixed constraint and focus our ingenuity on extracting more value from it. This is not about doing nothing; it is about a deliberate, engineering-led programme of work. We would begin with a deep characterisation of our current workloads, profiling not just average utilisation but the shape of demand over time. We would then implement dynamic scheduling and batching strategies that can pack inference jobs more efficiently, and we would explore model optimisation techniques such as quantization and distillation where they do not compromise quality. The direct financial benefit is real but modest; the larger prize is the reduction in latency variance and the improvement in reliability that comes from a system designed to handle its actual load profile rather than a theoretical peak.

When we weigh these options, the cost calculus is clear. Hardware acquisition is a large, sunk cost with a long payback period that depends on utilisation rates we cannot perfectly predict. Utilisation improvement, by contrast, is an investment in engineering time that yields compounding returns as our understanding of the system deepens. The latency implications also favour the utilisation path. Adding hardware can reduce average latency, but it does not address the tail latencies that often matter most for user experience. A well-tuned scheduling system, on the other hand, can dramatically smooth out those tails by preventing resource starvation.

Reliability is where the two paths diverge most sharply. More hardware means more components that can fail, more complex firmware to maintain, and a larger blast radius when something goes wrong. A utilisation-focused approach, while not without risk, tends to favour simpler, more composable systems that are easier to reason about and harder to break. The opportunity cost of the engineering hours spent on procurement and integration is also difficult to ignore. Those same engineers could be working on features that directly generate value for our users, rather than on plumbing that merely enables their work.

Reversibility is the final, and perhaps most decisive, factor. A decision to buy hardware is largely irreversible in any meaningful timeframe. We would be locked into a specific capacity level and a specific technology stack. A decision to improve utilisation, however, is highly reversible. If our experiments yield less than expected, we can stop, reassess, and still choose to purchase hardware later. If they yield more than expected, we have deferred a large capital outlay and gained a deeper understanding of our system. This optionality has real value, and it is asymmetrically in favour of the utilisation path.

Our recommendation is therefore to invest in a focused, time-boxed programme to improve the utilisation of our existing hardware. We should set clear, measurable targets for latency reduction and cost per inference, and we should revisit the hardware question after that programme has run its course. We acknowledge that this recommendation rests on the assumption that our current hardware is fundamentally adequate for our near-term needs. If that assumption proves wrong, we will have lost some time, but we will have lost it with the flexibility to course-correct. In a domain where the technology and our own requirements are both moving quickly, that flexibility is worth more than the raw capacity that a purchase would provide.
